faq.a: Your marginal rate is the rate on your last dollar of taxable income. It is the rate that applies to the next dollar you earn. Your effective rate is your total tax divided by your total gross income. It is the average rate you actually pay across all brackets.
faq.q: What is the difference between marginal and effective tax rates?

faq.a: No. Only the income that falls inside a bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate. Income in lower brackets keeps its lower rate. That is why your effective rate is always lower than your marginal rate when your income spans more than one bracket.
faq.q: Does my whole income get taxed at my marginal rate?

faq.a: A raise can push part of your income into a higher bracket, so the extra dollars are taxed at the higher rate. But only those extra dollars are taxed at the higher rate, and your take-home pay still goes up. The higher rate never applies to income you already earned in lower brackets.
faq.q: If a raise pushes me into a higher bracket, do I lose money?

faq.a: Yes. The 2026 figures come from IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32, and the 2027 figures come from IRS Revenue Procedure 2026-35, published November 5, 2026 with news release IR-2026-133. The rates are the same in both years: 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, and 37%.
